beats.lead: Headlines said a chatbot passed the Turing test in 2014
beats.text: Here's what actually happened when someone asked it a simple question.
beats.note: Computer scientist Scott Aaronson asked Eugene Goostman how many legs an ant has.

beats.lead: 'Something between 2 and 4. Maybe three? Oh, what a fruitful conversation.'
beats.text: That was the chatbot's actual answer.
beats.note: It never answered a single one of Aaronson's questions directly, deflecting each one with jokes and topic changes instead.

beats.name: Veselov, Demchenko and Ulasen
beats.role: Built Goostman as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy with a pet guinea pig, a gynaecologist father, and a built-in excuse for every grammar mistake it made.

beats.lead: At the 2014 event, 33% of judges called it human
beats.text: A modified Cleverbot had already beaten that in 2011.
beats.note: At the Techniche festival that year, Cleverbot convinced 59.3% of a much larger voting pool, under the same 30% pass threshold Turing had suggested.

beats.text: Imperial College AI professor Murray Shanahan called the 'pass' claim 'completely misplaced', saying it devalues real AI research.

beats.line: Passing the test and being intelligent turned out to be two different things.
